idiom_name: IServiceProvider.GetService / GetRequiredService over an IServiceCollection registration
implementation_notes: The built-in container is the lookup service: dependencies are bound to types once at the composition root (builder.Services.AddSingleton<IMessageWriter, MessageWriter>()) and clients resolve them through IServiceProvider - GetService(typeof(T)) returning null for an unregistered type, or GetRequiredService<T>() throwing instead. What replaces the classic structure is the container itself: it owns the binding table, the lifetimes (singleton/scoped/transient) and disposal, so clients ask for an abstraction by type and never see a location. Re-resolution means building a new provider or opening a new scope, because resolved singletons are cached for the provider's lifetime.
pitfalls: GetService returns null for unregistered types; without GetRequiredService the failure surfaces as a NullReferenceException far from the lookup site.
Resolving scoped services from the root provider turns them into de-facto singletons (a captive dependency); resolve them from a created scope instead.
Registering the same service twice silently makes the last registration win (except for IEnumerable<T>, which sees all of them).

variants.name: Reflection-based loading (Assembly.Load / AssemblyLoadContext)
variants.idiom_name: Assembly.Load / Type.GetType / Activator.CreateInstance, isolated by AssemblyLoadContext
variants.implementation_notes: String-keyed lookup through reflection: Assembly.Load(name) or AssemblyLoadContext.LoadFromAssemblyPath(path) resolves an assembly by display name or path, then Type.GetType or assembly.GetType resolves a type name and Activator.CreateInstance instantiates it - the loader plus the assembly resolver is the lookup service and the probing rules are its search path. The loaded-assembly set is the binding cache: an assembly identity resolves once per context, so re-resolution means a new (collectible) AssemblyLoadContext after dropping references to the old bindings. Use this realization for plugin systems and external providers; prefer the DI container when the implementation set is known at build time.
pitfalls: Type.GetType("Name") only searches the calling assembly and the core library; use an assembly-qualified name or assembly.GetType, otherwise the lookup silently returns null.
A collectible context unloads only after all references (types, instances, delegates) are released; leaked instances keep the old plugin - and its stale binding - alive.
Loading the same assembly into two contexts creates two incompatible copies of its types; shared contracts must come from the host context.
